Rational Drug Design from a hunch in a haystack to a molecule by design

How medicines are found: the shift from stumbling onto them empirically to engineering them against a known target — the discovery-to-development pipeline, and why each approved drug costs billions.

§0Part 1 · Importance of drug discovery

Why drug discovery matters

Drugs are the tools that turn devastating diseases into treatable conditions.

Before we ask how a drug is designed, it is worth remembering why the effort is worth billions of dollars and fifteen years. A single well-aimed molecule can rewrite the natural history of a disease — what killed a third of a continent becomes a footnote; a death sentence becomes a chronic condition managed with a daily pill. Dr Tietz opens with three case studies where a new therapeutic changed the entire treatment paradigm. Keep them in mind: they are the payoff that the rest of the lecture — the slow, expensive pipeline — is chasing.

🤔 Predict · before you read on

Around 1350 the plague killed one third to one half of everyone in Europe. Today it still exists — so why does it kill only ~100–200 people worldwide each year?

Not because the bacterium got weaker — because a drug changed the paradigm. Yersinia pestis is now readily killed by antibiotics such as penicillin and streptomycin, so a once-apocalyptic infection became a treatable one. The organism is the same; the tool in the clinician's hand is different. That is the whole point of drug discovery.

§0.1Penicillin & the plague

Infectious disease was the most common cause of pre-modern mortality. The plague (Black Death) claimed somewhere between one third and one half of the population of Europe between 1347 and 1351. Today, only 1,000–2,000 plague cases and ~100–200 deaths are reported globally each year — the disease is still with us, but antibiotics have stripped it of its terror. Penicillin is the emblem of that revolution, and Plate 0.1 shows why its chemistry works.

Label Key — the penicillin molecule
β-lactam ring
The four-membered ring bearing the C=O next to N. Its ring strain makes it highly reactive — this is the warhead that irreversibly acylates the bacterial enzyme, permanently switching it off.
Thiazolidine ring (S)
The five-membered sulfur-containing ring fused to the β-lactam. It holds the reactive ring in the right geometry and gives the class its characteristic shape and stability.
R–C(=O)–NH side chain
The acyl group that differs between penicillins (e.g. benzyl in penicillin G). Swapping R tunes the spectrum, acid stability and β-lactamase resistance — an early, real-world example of modifying one substituent to change a drug's properties.
–COOH
The carboxylic acid that mimics the terminal D-Ala–D-Ala of the bacterial cell-wall peptide, helping the drug dock into the enzyme's active site.
Reasoning · why does a small ring make a powerful antibiotic?

Penicillin is a structural mimic of the D-Ala–D-Ala end of the peptidoglycan chain that bacterial transpeptidases (penicillin-binding proteins) cross-link. The enzyme grabs penicillin thinking it is substrate — but the strained β-lactam ring then snaps open and covalently acylates the active-site serine, jamming the enzyme shut for good. Without cross-linking, the growing cell wall fails and the bacterium bursts. The lesson that echoes through this whole lecture: a drug's shape (fitting the active site) and its reactive chemistry (the warhead) together decide what it does.

Clinical / real-world

Because humans have no cell wall and no transpeptidase, penicillin is remarkably selectively toxic — it hits a bacterial target we simply do not possess. That selectivity is why it was safe enough to end the plague's dominance and remains a first-line antibiotic today. Resistance (β-lactamases that cleave the ring) is exactly why the R side chain gets re-engineered — the same design logic, run in an arms race.

§0.2HIV/AIDS — a death sentence made livable

The HIV/AIDS pandemic began in 1981 and has claimed over 44 million lives worldwide. Mortality is still high, but more people than ever now live with the virus — because we can hit the viral life-cycle at several points at once. Plate 0.2 shows two of those points: a protease inhibitor and an entry inhibitor.

Label Key — HIV antiretrovirals
Tipranavir — Protease Inhibitor
Binds the HIV protease enzyme, blocking the cleavage of viral polyproteins into working parts, so new virions cannot mature. Stops the assembly line after the cell is infected.
Maraviroc — Entry Inhibitor
A CCR5 antagonist: it blocks the host co-receptor HIV uses to fuse with and enter the cell, stopping infection before it starts. A different point in the life-cycle — which is exactly why it complements a protease inhibitor.
PrEP — Emtricitabine/tenofovir
Pre-exposure prophylaxis: two reverse-transcriptase inhibitors taken by uninfected people to prevent acquiring HIV. Particularly successful in Australia. (Structures shown on the source slide; the strategy, not just the molecule, is the innovation.)
Reasoning · why attack the same virus in several places?

A virus mutates fast; a single-target drug is quickly out-evolved by resistant strains. Hitting entry, reverse transcription and protease at once — combination antiretroviral therapy — means the virus would have to acquire several resistance mutations simultaneously, which is vanishingly unlikely. Each drug is a rationally designed key for a different lock in the same life-cycle; together they turn an untreatable, lethal infection into a manageable chronic condition.

Clinical / real-world

PrEP flips the timing of the intervention: instead of treating infection, it prevents acquisition in high-risk HIV-negative people. Australia's uptake has driven notable falls in new diagnoses — a reminder that who takes a drug and when can matter as much as the molecule itself, and that public-health strategy is part of the therapeutic paradigm.

§0.3COVID-19 — a pandemic met by design

The COVID-19 pandemic began in 2019 and has claimed over 7 million reported lives. Two kinds of drug blunted it: vaccines — which are themselves biologic drugs and a major contributor to falling infections and mortality — and a small-molecule antiviral, nirmatrelvir (Plate 0.3).

Label Key — nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid)
Nitrile (C≡N) warhead
Forms a reversible covalent bond with the catalytic cysteine of SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro), locking the enzyme. The reactive tip — analogous in role to penicillin's β-lactam.
Cyclopropyl-fused pyrrolidine core
A rigid scaffold shaped to fit the Mpro active-site pocket precisely — the product of structure-based (rational) design.
Lactam (2-oxopyrrolidine) side group
Mimics glutamine, the residue Mpro naturally cleaves after — so the drug is read by the enzyme as substrate and slots into the specificity pocket.
Trifluoroacetamide cap
The tert-butyl / CF₃ end tunes metabolic stability and binding; a modified 'cap' from the optimization campaign (compare Plate 3.3).
Reasoning · why is Mpro such a good target?

SARS-CoV-2 translates its genome as one long polyprotein that must be cut into functional pieces by its own main protease (Mpro). Block Mpro and the virus cannot make working proteins — replication stops. Crucially, humans have no enzyme like Mpro, so an Mpro inhibitor can be highly selective (again: hit a target the host does not have). Nirmatrelvir was designed against the solved 3D structure of Mpro — a textbook rational-design success, and we trace its optimization in §3.

Clinical / real-world

Nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid) reduces hospitalization and death by >80% in high-risk, unvaccinated outpatients, with benefit also to vaccinated, older patients — but only if given early, before viral load peaks. Timing again decides efficacy. And because Mpro inhibition is host-independent, the drug's activity does not depend on the patient's immune status the way a vaccine's protection does.

The take-home from all three: drugs are the tools clinicians use to turn devastating diseases into treatable conditions, and new therapeutics change treatment paradigms. Cancers and dementia are now leading causes of death and disability in Australia — the open question the lecture poses is how do we build the therapeutics that will change those paradigms too? The rest of this guide is the method for doing exactly that.

R Recall checklist — why drug discovery matters
  • Paradigm shift — drugs turn devastating diseases into treatable conditions; new therapeutics change treatment paradigms.
  • Penicillin warhead — the strained β-lactam ring irreversibly acylates bacterial transpeptidases (penicillin-binding proteins).
  • Plague then vs now — killed one third to one half of Europe (1347–51); now only ~100–200 deaths/year worldwide.
  • HIV combination — hit several life-cycle steps at once: protease inhibitor tipranavir + entry/CCR5 inhibitor maraviroc; PrEP = emtricitabine/tenofovir.
  • Nirmatrelvir target — SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro); cuts hospitalization/death by >80% in high-risk unvaccinated outpatients.
  • Selective toxicity theme — the best targets are ones the host does not have (cell-wall enzyme, viral protease).
§1Part 2 · Types of drug discovery

Empirical, rational & hybrid

Three routes to a drug — observe it, design it, or blend the two.

There are two philosophically opposite ways to find a drug, plus a pragmatic blend of both. You can start from an observed effect and work backwards (empirical), or start from a known target and build forwards (rational). The difference is not just historical trivia — it decides what you need to know before you begin, what can go wrong, and which is used most today. We foreshadowed the vocabulary in §0; here we make it precise.

§1.1Empirical (phenotypic) drug discovery

Empirical drug discovery — also called phenotypic drug discovery. Unpack the two words: empirical = based on real-world observation, direct experience, or physical testing; phenotypic = describing the observable traits or physical expression of a living organism. So you test candidates on a whole cell, tissue or animal and watch for the effect you want.

  • Approach — test drug candidates on whole cells, tissues or animals for the desired therapeutic response.
  • Target knowledge — does not require knowing the exact biological target or mechanism. You judge success by the phenotype, not the molecule it hits.
  • Discovery method — high-throughput screening of natural extracts or chemical libraries.
  • Key strength — uncovers unexpected mechanisms and often leads to successful first-in-class medicines.
  • Main limitation — "finding a needle in a haystack": the actual molecular target can be hard to identify, and it often leads to "dirty drugs" with multiple molecular targets.

All pre-modern drug discovery was empirical — but the approach is less common now. Its classic products are natural products: morphine (Plate 1.1), cocaine and aspirin, mined from plants long before anyone knew what they bound.

Label Key — morphine as an empirical archetype
Rigid fused-ring core
Five interlocked rings give a fixed 3D shape that happens to fit the μ-opioid receptor. Nobody designed this — it evolved in the opium poppy and was found by observing pain relief.
Basic N (N–CH₃)
The tertiary amine that is protonated at body pH and makes the key ionic contact in the receptor. Its presence explains the potent analgesia — the reason the empirical effect exists.
Phenol / hydroxyl groups
Hydrogen-bonding handles that anchor the drug in its binding pocket. Modifying these (e.g. acetylation → heroin) changes potency and lipophilicity — later, rational tuning of an empirical find.
Reasoning · why does phenotypic screening still find first-in-class drugs?

Because it makes no assumption about mechanism, a phenotypic screen can reward a molecule that works through a pathway nobody has thought of yet. Target-based screening can only find drugs against targets we already suspect — it is blind to the unknown. That freedom is empirical discovery's superpower: it uncovers unexpected mechanisms. The price is the "needle in a haystack" problem — you get an effect but not an address, and deconvoluting which molecule hits which protein is slow, which is why many empirical hits end up as poly-pharmacological "dirty drugs".

Memory hook · E before R

"Empirical = Effect first (you see it work, then hunt the target). Rational = Receptor first (you know the target, then build the molecule)."

Clinical / real-world

Nature is still a screening library: platforms like NatureBank hold over 20,000 natural-product extracts and 112,000 fractions derived from Australian plants, fungi and marine invertebrates, ready for high-throughput screening against any disease. Morphine, aspirin and cocaine prove the model works — and many empirical drugs are still in clinical use today, so this is not merely a historical curiosity.

§1.2Rational (molecular / target-based) drug discovery

Rational drug discovery — also called molecular or target-based drug discovery. Again, unpack the words: rationale = the fundamental, underlying reason or logical explanation; molecular = targeting specific molecules to achieve a therapeutic outcome; target-based = molecules designed to bind a specific molecular target. You begin by knowing the enemy and engineer a molecule to fit it.

  • Approach — use computer modelling to design molecules that bind a specific protein.
  • Target knowledge — requires a detailed 3D structure or clear understanding of the target. This is the defining difference from empirical.
  • Discovery method — computational molecular docking, structure-based drug design, and chemical synthesis tailored to active / binding sites.
  • Key strength — highly focused, allowing precise tuning of binding affinity and chemical properties.
  • Main limitation — two distinct failure modes (below).

Most modern drug discovery is rational drug design, enabled by advances in technology. But "rational" is not "guaranteed". A rational program can fail in two very different ways:

  • Failure of underlying pathway biology — the targeted pathway turns out to be regulated by complex host factors outside the isolated model. The molecule does exactly what you designed; the biology of the pathway was more complicated than assumed.
  • Failure of structural biology — the structural assumptions about the target were wrong, so the beautifully designed molecule does not actually fit.

The definitive cautionary tale is rofecoxib (VIOXX). Plate 1.2 shows the structural triumph that underlies it — how a drug can be engineered to fit COX-2 but not COX-1 — and Plate 1.3 shows the molecule itself.

Label Key — why COX-2 selectivity is possible
COX-1 pocket (green, panel A/B)
Note Ile434 / Ile532 / His513 lining a narrower channel. The bulky isoleucines wall off a side-pocket, so only a slim molecule fits.
COX-2 pocket (orange, panel A/B)
The equivalent residues are the smaller Val434 / Val532 plus Arg513, opening an extra side-pocket. This roomier site is the structural feature a designer can exploit.
Nonselective COX inhibitor (cyan, panel A)
A classic NSAID (e.g. ibuprofen-like) — small enough to bind both COX-1 and COX-2, so it blocks protective as well as inflammatory prostaglandins.
COX-2-selective inhibitor (magenta, panel B)
A bulkier 'coxib' with a group that reaches into COX-2's side-pocket — it fits COX-2 but is excluded from COX-1 (red cross). This is rational, structure-based selectivity in one picture.
Active site (labelled both)
The catalytic channel where arachidonic acid is normally converted to prostaglandins; blocking it stops prostaglandin synthesis.
Label Key — rofecoxib
Furanone (lactone) core
The central 5-membered ring that positions the two aryl groups — the rigid scaffold of the 'coxib' class.
Methylsulfonyl-phenyl group
The bulky –SO₂CH₃-bearing ring that reaches into COX-2's extra side-pocket (the Val523 gap) and is excluded by COX-1 — this is the feature that confers selectivity.
Second phenyl ring
Occupies the main hydrophobic channel, completing the fit into the active site shown in Plate 1.2.
Reasoning · a perfect molecule that still failed

Read Plates 1.2 and 1.3 together. The structural biology was great: rofecoxib was designed to slip into COX-2's roomier pocket and be blocked from COX-1, and it did precisely that — selectively sparing the stomach-protective COX-1 prostaglandins. The drugs "worked as intended from a molecular point of view". They failed because of an incomplete understanding of underlying pathway biology: selectively suppressing COX-2 also cut vascular prostacyclin (which resists clotting) while leaving platelet thromboxane (which promotes clotting) untouched — tipping the balance toward cardiovascular events. This is the failure-of-pathway-biology mode in the flesh: get the molecule right, get the wider biology wrong, and the drug is withdrawn.

Clinical / real-world

VIOXX was pulled from the market in 2004 after being linked to heart attacks and strokes — one of the largest drug withdrawals in history. The clinical lesson is humbling: on-target success is not the same as therapeutic success. A rationally designed drug can hit exactly what you aimed at and still harm patients because the target sits in a network you did not fully model — which is why early de-risking of pathway biology (§4) is now so heavily emphasised.

§1.3Hybrid drug discovery

Reality is rarely purely one or the other. In hybrid drug discovery, lead molecules are inspired by natural analogues rather than built from scratch by molecular docking — yet the work is still rational, because the goal remains to target a specific protein. Equally hybrid is the sequence: run a phenotypic screen → identify the target → rationally optimize a naturally-inspired parent compound. It borrows empirical inspiration and rational refinement.

Hybrid discovery is particularly popular for biologics — peptides and proteins — including the development of semaglutide (sold as Ozempic), shown in Plate 1.4.

Label Key — engineering GLP-1 into semaglutide
Native GLP-1 (half-life 1–2 min)
The natural incretin hormone. Powerful but useless as a drug because DPP-4 chews it up within minutes (arrow marks the DPP-4 cleavage site at position 2).
Aib substitution (red bead)
Position 2's Ala is swapped for Aib (α-aminoisobutyric acid). This non-natural residue makes the peptide unrecognisable to DPP-4, blocking the fast cleavage — a rational fix to a known liability.
C18 diacid fatty-acid chain + Linker (at Lys)
A long dicarboxylic fatty acid attached via a linker to a lysine. It binds albumin in the blood, hiding the peptide from clearance and stretching half-life to ~165 h (weekly dosing).
Semaglutide (half-life 165 h)
The finished hybrid: natural GLP-1 backbone + two designed modifications. Nature supplied the lead; rational engineering made it a viable weekly medicine.
Reasoning · why is hybrid the natural home of biologics?

You cannot easily invent a 30-residue signalling peptide from a blank docking screen — evolution has already built one that binds the receptor perfectly. So for biologics it is far smarter to start from the natural ligand (empirical inspiration) and then rationally patch its weaknesses — proteolytic instability, rapid renal clearance. Semaglutide is the paradigm: two targeted edits (Aib to dodge DPP-4; a fatty-acid to grab albumin) convert a hormone with a 1–2 minute half-life into a once-weekly drug. That is discovery that is both empirical in origin and rational in execution.

Clinical / real-world

Semaglutide's long half-life is what makes a once-weekly injection feasible for type-2 diabetes and obesity — patient adherence lives or dies on dosing frequency. It shows that pharmacokinetic engineering (how long the drug lasts) can be as decisive for real-world success as the pharmacodynamic binding itself — a theme that returns in the lead-optimization stage (§3).

Empirical vs rational vs hybrid at a glance
FeatureEmpirical / phenotypicRational / target-basedHybrid
Starting pointAn observed effect on cells/tissue/animalsA known molecular target's 3D structureA natural analogue / a phenotypic hit whose target is then found
Target known first?NoYes — requiredEnds up targeting a specific protein
MethodHigh-throughput screening of extracts/librariesDocking, structure-based design, tailored synthesisNatural inspiration + rational optimization
StrengthFinds unexpected mechanisms; first-in-classFocused; precise affinity/property tuningBest of both; suits complex molecules
Main risk"Needle in a haystack"; dirty drugsWrong pathway biology OR wrong structural biologyInherits target-based risks
Typical productsMorphine, cocaine, aspirinSmall-molecule inhibitors (rofecoxib, nirmatrelvir)Biologics — semaglutide (Ozempic)
R Recall checklist — types of drug discovery
  • Empirical = phenotypic — test on whole cells/tissue/animals; no target knowledge needed; judged by observable effect.
  • Empirical strength/limit — finds first-in-class / unexpected mechanisms, but "needle in a haystack" → dirty drugs.
  • Rational = molecular/target-based — computer-model a molecule to fit a protein; requires the 3D structure.
  • Two rational failure modes — wrong pathway biology (host factors) or wrong structural biology (bad structural assumptions).
  • Rofecoxib lesson — structural biology great, failed on pathway biology (cardiovascular) → on-target ≠ safe.
  • Hybrid — natural-analogue inspiration + rational optimization; the home of biologics, e.g. semaglutide (Aib blocks DPP-4; C18 diacid binds albumin → 165 h).
§2Part 3 · Types of drugs

Types of drugs — the size ladder

From a 500 g/mol pill to a 250,000 g/mol gene therapy.

Before mapping the pipeline, it helps to know what kind of thing we are trying to make — because size dictates almost everything downstream: how you discover it, how you synthesise it, and how it gets into the body. Plate 2.1 lays the classes out from smallest to largest.

Label Key — the drug-type ladder
Small molecules (<500 g/mol)
The classic 'pill'. Small enough to be orally absorbed and to slip into enzyme active sites — the natural home of rational design (rofecoxib, nirmatrelvir).
Peptides (<5,000 g/mol)
Short amino-acid chains (e.g. semaglutide). More specific than small molecules but usually injected, since the gut would digest them.
Proteins (<50,000 g/mol)
Folded functional proteins (e.g. insulin, enzymes). Highly specific; require biological manufacture and cold-chain handling.
Antibodies (~150,000 g/mol)
Monoclonal antibodies — exquisitely selective for one epitope. ~300× heavier than a small molecule; the workhorse biologic in oncology and immunology.
Gene therapies (>250,000 g/mol)
The largest class — deliver genetic material to correct disease at its source. Most complex to design, make and deliver.
The bridge: Disease Mechanism → Unmet Clinical Need
The overarching arc — Drug Discovery (finding/optimizing the molecule) hands over to Drug Development (turning it into a usable, approved medicine).
Reasoning · why does size decide the route?

Bigger molecules are more specific (more surface to make selective contacts) but harder to deliver. A small molecule under 500 g/mol can diffuse across the gut wall and cell membranes — so it can be a pill and can reach intracellular targets. Peptides, proteins, antibodies and gene therapies are too large and too fragile to survive digestion, so they are generally injected and act on extracellular or surface targets. This is also why rational docking dominates the small-molecule end while hybrid/biological methods dominate the large-molecule end (§1). Size is not a label — it is a constraint that shapes the whole program.

Clinical / real-world

The size of the drug determines the prescription in your hand: a small molecule is a daily tablet; an antibody or gene therapy is a hospital infusion. It also drives cost — biologics are far more expensive to manufacture (living-cell factories, cold chain) than a chemically synthesised small molecule, which feeds directly into the economics of §4.

R Recall checklist — types of drugs
  • Small molecules — <500 g/mol; orally absorbed; classic rational-design targets.
  • Peptides — <5,000 g/mol; e.g. semaglutide; usually injected.
  • Proteins — <50,000 g/mol; biologically manufactured.
  • Antibodies — ~150,000 g/mol; highly selective monoclonals.
  • Gene therapies — >250,000 g/mol; largest and most complex class.
  • Size → route — bigger = more specific but injected; smaller = oral and can reach intracellular targets.
§3Part 4 · Stages of drug discovery

Stages of drug discovery

Target → Hit → Lead → Candidate → IND → the clinic.

Now the method itself. Rational drug design involves using the known structure and function of a biological target to methodically invent a new, precisely fitting drug molecule. Plate 3.1 is the map you should be able to draw from memory — the whole journey from a disease mechanism to a launched medicine, with the time each stage takes.

Label Key — the pipeline (read left to right)
Target hypothesis — usually decades
Identify the receptor/enzyme/nucleic acid behind the disease. The slowest, most fundamental step — the science that makes everything after it possible.
Target-to-hit — ~1 year → Hit
Map the target's 3D active site and find initial molecules/fragments that bind. Produces the first milestone: a Hit.
Hit-to-lead — ~1.5 years → Lead
Screen thousands of hit-derived compounds and improve binding affinity and fit (PD). Produces the Lead.
Lead optimization — ~1 year → Candidate
Tune charge/shape so the body can safely absorb, distribute and process it (PK). Produces the drug Candidate.
Preclinical — ~1.5 years → IND
Test in the lab and ≥2 animal models for safety/toxicity; success triggers the IND application to enter humans.
Phase I / II / III — ~1.5 / 2.5 / 2.5 years
Human trials: safety in a few (I), efficacy/dose in more (II), confirmation in large populations (III). The expensive end.
Submission to launch — ~1.5 years
Regulatory review and approval, turning a proven candidate into a prescribable medicine.
The four coloured bands
Disease Mechanism → Drug Discovery → Drug Development → Clinical Development — the phases the sub-steps belong to.
Memory hook · the milestone chain

"Hit, Lead, Candidate, IND — Have Lunch, Continue INside." Each named point is the output of the stage before it: target-to-hit gives a Hit, hit-to-lead gives a Lead, lead optimization gives a Candidate, preclinical gives the IND filing.

§3.1The rational-design steps in detail

Trace Plate 3.1 stage by stage — each has a specific job.

Target hypothesis

Find a specific cell receptor, enzyme or nucleic acid linked to a disease, and confirm that modifying this target will safely treat the condition. Getting this wrong is the "failure of pathway biology" from §1 — so validation here is everything.

Target-to-hit

Map the three-dimensional shape and active site of the target biomacromolecule using lab techniques like X-ray crystallography or computational tools (including AI systems), then search for initial "hit" molecules or chemical fragments that can bind — both computationally and in the lab. Plate 3.2 is what this looks like: a fragment nestled in the mapped active site of the target protein.

Label Key — a target structure with a bound hit
Protein surface / ribbon (orange)
The target biomacromolecule's fold and its active-site pocket, solved by X-ray crystallography (or AI-assisted modelling). You cannot design a fit without this map.
Bound fragment / hit (stick model in the pocket)
An initial small molecule shown occupying the site — the physical evidence that a Hit binds where you want it to.
Neighbouring domain (green)
Adjacent structural context that can shape or constrain the binding site — a reminder that the pocket does not exist in isolation.

Hit-to-lead generation

Use virtual and lab-based screening to test thousands of compounds designed on the "hit structure", and modify the chemical structure of the hit to improve its binding strength (affinity) and fit — this is the pharmacodynamic (PD) side of the work. Plate 3.3 shows exactly this campaign for the COVID drug from §0: each arrow is a deliberate edit to one part of the molecule, trading measured properties until a viable Lead emerges.

Label Key — reading an SAR optimization map
P1 / P2 / P3 units (green labels)
The distinct sub-regions of the inhibitor, each occupying a different sub-pocket of the protease. Editing one at a time isolates its effect — systematic, not random.
Arrows: "modifying the warhead / P2 / P3 unit / P3 cap"
Each rational edit. The molecule is rebuilt piece by piece from parent (PF-00835231) to nirmatrelvir (PF-07321332).
EC₅₀ & Kᵢ (red/blue values)
Potency measures — how tightly and effectively it inhibits SARS-CoV-2 Mpro. Lower = better; the PD target of hit-to-lead.
oral F and Fₐ×F_g
Oral bioavailability — the fraction of an oral dose that reaches the blood. Note it climbs to ~50% by nirmatrelvir; this is a PK property (spills into lead optimization).
HLM CLint
Intrinsic clearance against human liver microsomes — a proxy for metabolic stability. Lower means the liver destroys it more slowly, so it lasts longer.
↑ ↓ ~ activity annotations
At each step, inhibitory activity, metabolic stability, antiviral activity and oral bioavailability go up, down or stay the same — the explicit trade-offs a medicinal chemist balances.

Lead optimization

Now shift from "does it bind?" to "can the body handle it?". Adjust traits like electrical charge and shape to make sure the body can absorb, distribute, and process the drug safely — the pharmacokinetic (PK) side. (Note: in some modern programs, hit-to-lead and lead optimization are integrated — you can see PD and PK numbers optimized together in Plate 3.3.) The output is the drug Candidate.

Preclinical and clinical testing

Test the optimized compound in laboratory and animal settings for safety and toxicity — in at least two animal models. Move forward into human clinical trials if the drug proves effective and non-toxic, via an Investigational New Drug (IND) application. From there it enters the clinical phases charted in Plate 3.1.

Reasoning · why is the order Target → Hit → Lead → Candidate not negotiable?

Each stage de-risks a different unknown and gates the next. You must know the target exists and matters before it is worth finding a molecule; you need a hit that binds before it is worth spending on making it bind better (the Lead); a lead is worthless if the body destroys or cannot absorb it, so you optimize PK into a Candidate; and no candidate touches a human until animals show it is safe. The logic is a funnel: cheapest, most fundamental questions first, most expensive commitments last — which, as §4 shows, is exactly what the economics demand.

Memory hook · PD then PK

"Hit-to-lead = Does it stick? (PD). Lead optimization = Can the body Kope with it? (PK)." First make it bind well, then make it behave well in the body.

Clinical / real-world

The two-animal-model rule and the IND gate exist because history is full of drugs that looked perfect in a test tube and harmed the first humans who took them. They are the regulatory embodiment of the whole "de-risk before you commit" ethos — and nirmatrelvir (Plates 0.3, 3.3) shows the payoff: a molecule engineered stepwise against a solved protease structure, all the way to a real medicine that cut COVID deaths.

In summary: rational drug discovery = selection of a target, discovery of hit compounds, development and optimization of a lead compound, and testing in pre-clinical and clinical models — and it thrives on bold ideas and close cooperation between biologists, chemists and clinicians.

R Recall checklist — stages of drug discovery
  • Target hypothesis — find a receptor/enzyme/nucleic acid linked to disease and confirm modifying it safely treats the condition (takes decades).
  • Target-to-hit — map the 3D active site (X-ray crystallography/AI) and find binding hits/fragments.
  • Hit-to-lead — screen thousands of hit-based compounds; improve affinity & fit (PD) → Lead.
  • Lead optimization — tune charge/shape for absorption/distribution/processing (PK) → Candidate (often integrated with hit-to-lead).
  • Preclinical — safety/toxicity in ≥2 animal models; if safe & effective, file the IND to enter humans.
  • Milestone chain — Hit → Lead → Candidate → IND, each the output of the stage before it.
§4Part 5 · The drug discovery process

Cost, time & attrition

Why every approved drug carries a billion-dollar price tag it never earned alone.

The pipeline of §3 is not just slow — it is brutally expensive and it fails far more often than it succeeds. Understanding the numbers explains almost every strategic decision in the industry, from why companies kill projects early to why they are pouring money into AI. These are the figures to commit to memory.

🤔 Predict · before you read on

If it costs on the order of US$1.5–3 bn to bring one drug through Phase III, roughly how many other projects were abandoned for each one that got approved?

As a rule of thumb, at least 99 other projects were abandoned somewhere along the pipeline for every approved drug — a success rate of about 1 in 100. That is why each approval is so costly: the winner has to pay for its ninety-nine dead siblings.
  • Cost — approximate cost to develop a drug to the end of Phase III = US$1.5 bn to US$3.0 bn.
  • Time — the process takes between 10 and 15 years.
  • Cost escalates along the pathway — Target, Hit, Lead and Pre-clinical are relatively cheap; Phase III trials are very expensive. Phase II and Phase III failure of a candidate is very costly.
  • Attrition — as a rule of thumb, for every approved drug, at least 99 other projects were abandoned somewhere along the pipeline.
  • De-risk early — early de-risking of projects is essential; pharmaceutical companies increasingly integrate AI systems into every part of the process to increase the likelihood of regulatory approval.
Reasoning · why does cost escalate, and why is late failure catastrophic?

Early stages are cheap because they are small: a docking run or a fragment screen costs little. Clinical trials are expensive because they are large and human — thousands of patients, years of monitoring, manufacturing to regulatory standard. So the spending curve rises steeply toward Phase III. That geometry is why late failure is ruinous: if a drug dies at the target or hit stage you have lost a little; if it dies in Phase III you have already spent nearly the entire ~US$1.5–3 bn and have nothing to show for it. The rational response is to de-risk early — kill doomed projects while they are still cheap — which is precisely why AI is being pushed into every stage to spot failures sooner.

Worked example · why each approved drug "costs" ~US$1.5–3 bn

The headline cost is per approved drug — but the money is spent across all the failures too. Let's see how a ~1-in-100 success rate and cost-escalation combine to produce a billion-dollar figure. Take round numbers consistent with the slide.

  1. State the success rate. The rule of thumb is ≥99 abandoned : 1 approved, i.e. a success probability of about p = 1/100 = 1%. So to get 1 approval you must start roughly 100 projects.
  2. Recognise where the money goes. Cost escalates along the pathway: the many projects that die early (Target/Hit/Lead/Pre-clinical) are individually cheap, while the few that reach Phase II/III are individually very expensive. So the total is dominated by the handful of late, costly attempts — not by the 90-odd cheap early deaths.
  3. Model it simply. Suppose of ~100 starts, ~90 die cheaply at say US$10 m each, and ~10 reach expensive late trials at say US$150 m each (only one of which is ultimately approved). Early spend: 90 × $10 m = $0.9 bn. Late spend: 10 × $150 m = $1.5 bn.
  4. Total the portfolio cost for that single success. $0.9 bn + $1.5 bn = $2.4 bn spent to yield one approved drug.
  5. Attribute it to the winner. Divide the whole portfolio's spend by the number of approvals: $2.4 bn ÷ 1 = $2.4 bn per approved drug — landing squarely in the slide's US$1.5–3 bn range.

Answer: the ~US$1.5–3 bn is not what one molecule cost — it is the whole portfolio's spend divided across the ~1% that succeed. High per-attempt cost (esp. late trials) × ~1-in-100 attrition = a billion-dollar price on every approval. (Illustrative figures — the point is the structure, not exact inputs.)

Memory hook · the three numbers

"1.5–3, 10–15, 99." ~US$1.5–3 bn to end of Phase III, 10–15 years, and 99 projects abandoned per approval (~1% success).

Clinical / real-world

This economics is why new medicines are expensive and why rare-disease drugs can seem astronomically priced — the same ~US$1.5–3 bn must be recouped from far fewer patients. It also explains the industry's pivot to AI-assisted discovery: even a modest improvement in early de-risking (killing losers before Phase III) shifts the attrition maths and can save hundreds of millions per approval. For patients, better odds upstream ultimately mean more paradigm-changing drugs like those in §0 reaching the clinic.

R Recall checklist — cost, time & attrition
  • Cost to end of Phase III — US$1.5 bn to US$3.0 bn.
  • Timeline — 10 to 15 years from target to launch.
  • Cost escalation — Target/Hit/Lead/Pre-clinical are cheap; Phase III is very expensive; Phase II/III failure is very costly.
  • Attrition rule of thumb — ≥99 projects abandoned per approved drug (~1% success).
  • Why each approval costs billions — the winner must pay for the ~99 failures, and the late failures cost the most.
  • Strategic response — de-risk early; integrate AI across every stage to raise the odds of approval.
